headline: Massachusetts-grown cranberries are headed for school cafeterias
dek: A new state partnership with Ocean Spray will put reduced-sugar dried cranberries made entirely from in-state fruit into participating K–12 meal programs this fall.
body: Massachusetts students will soon have a locally grown snack option in school cafeterias as the state works with Ocean Spray Cranberries Inc. to bring dried cranberries made entirely from Massachusetts fruit into participating K–12 meal programs. The [state announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-announces-massachusetts-grown-cranberries-for-schools-across-the-state) describes the partnership as part of the Commonwealth’s broader farm-to-school effort and says the first product will be available to participating districts in October.

The program is designed around the way public schools already buy food. The Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education awarded Ocean Spray a contract to process reduced-sugar dried cranberries for districts that participate in the U.S. Department of Agriculture Foods Distribution Program. That means the initiative is not a statewide retail launch or a requirement that every school add cranberries to its menu. Districts will decide whether and when to order through the existing distribution system.

For the 2026–27 school year, districts will order through Gold Star Foods, the state-contracted warehouse and distributor in Canton. The standard delivery fee will be waived, according to the state, a practical detail that can matter to food-service directors working with tight budgets and storage schedules. The products will be available exclusively to Massachusetts K–12 school districts through that program, so families will need to check their own district’s menu or food-service notices to know whether the snack is being served.

The first item is a Fruit Punch flavored Craisins dried-cranberry pouch scheduled to arrive in October. A Raspberry Lemonade flavored version is planned for February 2027. Both are part of Ocean Spray’s reformulated 1.16-ounce school platform and were developed to meet updated USDA requirements for added sugars in school meals. Ocean Spray’s [school nutrition materials](https://www2.oceanspray.com/foodservice/segments/schools) describe the company’s broader K–12 food-service line, while the state announcement supplies the Massachusetts-specific terms. The state says the Fruit Punch product contains 12 grams of sugar, compared with 24 grams in Ocean Spray’s original dried-cranberry product, and that each pouch provides a half-cup of fruit under the product’s serving calculation.

The Massachusetts sourcing requirement is the central feature of the agreement. Ocean Spray has verified that 100% of the cranberries used in the two school products will be grown and harvested in the Commonwealth. That connects a familiar packaged food to farms in southeastern Massachusetts, where cranberry production is concentrated. The [Massachusetts Department of Agricultural Resources’ October proclamation](https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-proclaims-october-as-massachusetts-cranberry-month) identifies cranberries as the state’s official berry and marks the start of the annual harvest season.

The state’s education announcement says cranberries are Massachusetts’ top agricultural food commodity crop, supporting more than 6,400 jobs and generating more than $1.7 billion in economic impact, with about 11,500 acres of commercial bogs. Those figures are presented by the state as a measure of the industry’s importance; they do not mean that the new school contract will produce a comparable share of that economic activity. The immediate effect is narrower: it gives districts another locally sourced item they can purchase through a familiar federal food channel.

The partnership also illustrates why processing and distribution are as important as farming in local-food programs. Fresh cranberries are seasonal, while a shelf-stable dried product can be portioned, shipped and stored for school service. By using Ocean Spray’s processing operation and the USDA Foods network, the state is trying to fit a Massachusetts crop into the operational requirements of cafeterias rather than asking every district to build a new local supply chain from scratch.

The rollout comes as Massachusetts continues its universal free school-meals program and as state officials promote local procurement as a way to support farmers while improving school food. The cranberry products are not a new benefit that changes student eligibility, and the announcement does not say how many districts will participate. The next measurable step will be district orders and menu postings this fall, followed by the second flavor’s planned arrival in February. For growers, schools and families, the test will be whether a state-specific product can move from a seasonal crop into regular, affordable cafeteria service.
location: Massachusetts cranberry farms and K–12 schools statewide
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Massachusetts-grown cranberries coming to school meals
seoDescription: A Massachusetts-Ocean Spray partnership will bring reduced-sugar dried cranberries made from in-state fruit to participating K–12 schools.
